newsitem.title: USA: IMF still sees monetary role for gold - WGC.
newsitem.headline: IMF still sees monetary role for gold - WGC.

text.p: Despite recent plans to sell a small amount of its gold to fund a Third World debt relief program, International Monetary Fund (IMF) has come to recognize many of the advantages of gold as a valuable monetary asset, said Robert Pringle, head of World Gold Council's (WGC) Center for Public Policy Studies.
"The proposal to sell a small amount of the Fund's gold does not in the least imply the Fund now has a negative attitude to gold," Pringle told Gold and Silver Institute's annual conference here.
"The IMF's latest annual report makes this clear," he said.

IMF's annual report says gold is "a fundamental strength" in its balance sheet, adding, "the Fund's gold holdings provide the Fund with operational manoeuvrability, both as regards its policies on the use of its resources and through adding credibility to the level of the Fund's precautionary balances."

IMF's annual report also notes "the Fund has a systemic responsibility, given it is the second-largest official holder in the world, with about 10 percent of total official gold stocks of member countries."

Official holdings of gold by governments and international institutions are estimated at about 36,000 tonnes of gold, about a quarter of the world's estimated above-ground stocks of 129,000 tonnes at the end of 1995.
The dispute over the IMF plan to sell some of its gold in the past year demonstrates that many central banks still believe gold has a key role to play in the world monetary system, Pringle argued.

Taking up the suggestion of U.K. Chancellor of the Exchequer, Kenneth Clarke, and supported by the U.S. and other countries, the IMF managing director, Michel Camdessus, last year campaigned for the Fund's members to agree to a sale of five million ounces of IMF gold to finance debt relief for poor countries, if it could not obtain the needed cash from contributions from IMF member countries.
But Camdessus failed to get the required 85 percent majority among IMF members.
Germany led the opposition to the plan and remains opposed, Pringle noted, and even if Germany climbs down, the plan will still need U.S. Congressional approval.
"So two decisions will still be needed before sales can go ahead - a decision by the Fund's executive board that bilateral contributions are not enough and a decision by Congress," Pringle said.

"In sum, I believe this dispute has underlined again the fact there is indeed a monetary role for gold today," he said. "Germany's stand has proved that Europe's largest and most powerful country takes this subject seriously, seriously enough indeed to risk an open confrontation with the world's only remaining superpower."
